extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students and instructors (readers of expository/combinatorics material)
extracted.subtask_description: An expository article in discrete mathematics (combinatorics/graph theory/poset topology) intended to teach definitions, theorems, and pedagogical practice for undergraduate courses and instructors. Includes descriptions of graph storage representations, inclusion–exclusion and Möbius inversion, poset topology, and a piece on guided group discovery pedagogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vector-based adjacency list: sizes of p and e
rubrics_metrics.description: The size of vector e is twice the number of edges in the graph and the size of p is one more than the number of vertices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This representation stores adjacency information in two vectors p and e; p holds pointers (indices) into e. Footnote: the vectors p and e can be combined into one longer vector by adding n+1 to each element of p and prepending it to e.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree computation from vector-based adjacency list
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition of p makes it easy to calculate the degree of a vertex since the degree of vertex i is just pŒi 1/2, where n is the number of vertices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The surrounding explanation links the p-array entries for successive vertices to compute the number of incident edge endpoints; (OCR in source garbled the precise formula). The technique makes degree queries straightforward from the p array boundaries for vertex i.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memory-efficiency criterion for vector-based adjacency lists
rubrics_metrics.description: If the number of edges in the graph is less than n^2, this method of storage takes less room than using a traditional adjacency matrix.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use vector-based adjacency lists when graphs are sparse relative to n^2. The method is especially useful in languages without pointers (e.g., COBOL and FORTRAN). However, it is noted that pointer-based representations are generally easier to deal with in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical adoption note for vector-based representation
rubrics_metrics.description: This method of representation is not much used since the method based on pointers ... is generally easier to deal with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose pointer-based linked lists for general-purpose graph algorithms in pointer-friendly languages; use vector-based lists when pointers are unavailable or when memory layout advantages are needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linked adjacency lists: traversal and mutability
rubrics_metrics.description: For each vertex v in the graph, the elements in adj(v) are placed in a linked list. It is easy to traverse these lists to find all of the vertices adjacent to v. Since it is easy to add and delete elements in these lists, it is easy to add and delete edges in the graph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A vector of n pointers is used to gain access to the individual linked lists. This is described as the most common way to represent graphs in standard graph algorithms because of its dynamism (efficient edge insertions/deletions) and traversal convenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjacency-list pointer-vector requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A vector of n pointers is used to gain access to the individual linked lists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implementation detail: maintain an array (or vector) of head pointers indexed by vertex to access that vertex's adjacency linked list; this supports O(degree(v)) traversal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability condition for the Principle of Inclusion–Exclusion (PIE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let A1, ..., An be finite sets. Then |A1 ∪ ... ∪ An| = (alternating sum over intersections) — i.e., the classical PIE formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PIE applies to finite sets and counts union size by alternating sums of sizes of intersections. The exposition emphasizes undercounting and overcounting corrections and shows PIE as the special case of Möbius inversion on the Boolean lattice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of PIE to Euler's totient function
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the PIE to derive a formula for the Euler totient function φ(n). Theorem 2.2: If n = ∏ p_i^{α_i} then φ(n) = n ∏_{i=1}^k (1 - 1/p_i).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct Ai as numbers ≤ n divisible by prime p_i; apply PIE to count integers coprime to n (totatives). The article shows the derivation step-by-step and cites elementary number theory references for background.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and basic property of the classical Möbius function
rubrics_metrics.description: Define μ(d) for a positive integer d by (source text wording): '1/r . 0 if d is the product of r distinct primes, otherwise.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although OCR in the source is imperfect, the intent is to define μ(d) (the classical Möbius function) in terms of the prime factorization of d and then to use it in the summation φ(n) = ∑_{d|n} μ(d) (n/d). The Möbius function is central to classical Möbius inversion on the lattice of divisors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classical Möbius inversion applicability (divisor lattice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 3.1 (Classical Möbius inversion): For integer-valued functions f and g on positive integers, f(n)=∑_{d|n} g(d) iff g(n)=∑_{d|n} μ(d) f(n/d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This equivalence is the discrete-number-theoretic instance of Möbius inversion and follows from properties of the divisor lattice D. The article frames this as a special case of generalized Möbius inversion on posets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for generalized Möbius inversion on posets
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalized Möbius inversion: let P be a locally finite lower-bounded (or upper-bounded) poset. For complex-valued functions f and g on P, f(x)=∑_{y≤x} g(y) iff g(x)=∑_{y≤x} f(y) μ_P(y,x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorems 5.3 and 5.4 state lower-bounded and upper-bounded Möbius inversion. Key conditions: P must be locally finite and have the appropriate bound (minimum or maximum) so that the sums are finite and the zeta function is invertible in the incidence algebra.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incidence algebra and Möbius function existence criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: For any locally finite poset P, the zeta function ζ_P is invertible in the incidence algebra I(P), and its inverse is the Möbius function μ_P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: incidence functions on intervals with convolution product form an associative algebra; invertibility of ζ_P (value 1 on intervals) yields μ_P via recursive formula (11). Use incidence-algebra viewpoint for conceptual clarity, though the recursion can be used directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topological interpretation condition for μ_P
rubrics_metrics.description: If P is bounded, then μ_P(0,1) (i.e., μ_P evaluated on the minimal and maximal elements) equals the reduced Euler characteristic of the order complex Δ(P\{0,1}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This connects combinatorial Möbius functions to topology: compute μ_P by computing homology/Euler characteristic of the order complex (simplicial complex of chains). The article points to lexicographic shellability and further topological techniques for refined invariants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course prerequisite standard for guided group discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Prerequisites for Bogart's course: comfort with sets, functions, and algebraic notation (including some summation notation); some experience with reading (and perhaps doing) proofs; and, ideally, a modest exposure to mathematical induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flahive notes that typical students may not meet these prerequisites; adaptation of materials and instruction is necessary for required courses with larger, less-prepared enrollments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem completion expectation (student requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students are expected to complete 90% of the problems, with the proviso that they should not systematically avoid the more challenging problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The notes use symbols to mark problems (essential, motivational, summary, especially interesting, difficult) to help students and instructors prioritize. The 90% target is a concrete completion/engagement metric for the group-discovery approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment policy to ensure individual accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Most of the course grade comes from non-group work, including traditional in-class exams and the expectation that final solutions will be completed without consultation or collaboration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use group work for in-class discovery and learning but assess individuals with closed-book exams and require independent final write-ups to ensure individual mastery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructor guidance and classroom management criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructor must balance giving students sufficient time to work successfully in groups and ensuring students are satisfactorily progressing through the material; use selective and thoughtful large-group discussion; guide some groups to push ahead to more difficult problems; model good group dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large-group discussion can be used to model productive listening and problem-solving without an all-knowing participant. Instructor interventions should be selective, facilitate progress, and maintain overall class pacing while preserving student responsibility for learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation criterion for larger/lower-prep classes
rubrics_metrics.description: When adapting Bogart's guided-discovery notes to required courses with larger enrollments and students with weaker preparation, modifications to the notes and class implementation are necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flahive describes adjusting problem sets, instructor facilitation, and support structures (e.g., selective grouping, additional scaffolding) to retain the benefits of discovery learning in larger/less-prepared cohorts; the adaptation is iterative and was supported by NSF-funded work.
